The builtin parser_for/encode_for is seriously limited. It's basically only usable for JSON.
For example, there's no way to configure whether a List(U8) should be emitted as bstr (bytes blob) or [* uint] (list of U8 — the * means in CDDL that it can have an arbitrary length). https://github.com/roc-lang/roc/issues/11660
See the issue for more details on the problem.
This can be worked around by decoding the CBOR into an AST, then manually filling in the struct fields.
But this wastes memory, because the AST is stored separately, instead of directly decoding data into the struct fields.

Still trying to get my head round the parser api myself, so - partially for my own understanding - couldn't this be implemented with a wrapper type for the byte blob around List(U8)? The wrapper type would have to have a custom parser_for and encoder_for, which would expect from the 'generic' format some Encoding.parse_blob and Encoding.encode_blob respectively, which return and take List(U8). In practice the format wouldn't be generic because you would use it exclusively with your Cbor format, in which you would implement encode_blob/parse_blob.
This solution would require unpacking it everywhere in the program. An ideal serialization library would not require modifying the program everywhere in order to configure the serialized output.
Yeh I get that for sure. I mean, the unpacking would be free computationally, if not ergonomically?

Yes, but it's really a bad idea to write my program code differently because some serialization library needs it that way.

If this is the case, even a manual serialization is better, since that's concentrating the added complexity at the parse/encode function, and not creeping into the whole program.

Does it creep into the whole program though? I imagine ser/de typically being at the shell of your code, and only at that periphery do you need to convert your specific List(U8) into Bytes so that the Cbor format can dispatch to the right encoder/decoder
It's possible, but then I would need a different struct type, with the only difference being the given field.

Yeh that's what I arrived at too. It would be more ergonomic if there was a way to update records but also change the type like : record_for_cbor = {..internal, data: internal.data |> Blob.from_list()}. For more nested records it would be less pleasant.

Is https://www.roc-lang.org/examples/EncodeDecode/README the relevant doc here?

I'm kinda curious how you would use CBOR data in a Roc program. If you know the data types in advance, then I think you could use nominal types like the README says? If you don't know the data types in advance, then I don't know what advantages you get from using Roc.
Also https://github.com/roc-lang/roc/blob/main/docs/langref/static-dispatch.md#parsing-and-encoding

I'm kinda curious how you would use CBOR data in a Roc program. If you know the data types in advance, then I think you could use nominal types like the README says? If you don't know the data types in advance, then I don't know what advantages you get from using Roc.

MyType := {
  blob_field: List(U8) # This stores a blob, e.g. a binary file.
  list_of_ints: List(U8) # This stores actual numbers.
}

How would you achieve that blob_field gets serialized as bstr, while list_of_ints gets serialized as [* uint]?

notramo said:

How would you achieve that blob_field gets serialized as bstr, while list_of_ints gets serialized as [* uint]?

I think opaque types are one option.

Blob := { bytes : List U8 }
That's what I want to avoid. Why change my entire program just to configure an encoder?

notramo said:

That's what I want to avoid. Why change my entire program just to configure an encoder?

I don't know your use case or your programming style well enough to answer that question. But I think you'd be wise to just model Blobs as Blobs with or without encoding considerations. Presumably you're doing something useful with the Blob, so even Blob is kinda low-level. I don't understand why you would avoid nominal types in a language where that's a major selling point.
The problem is that a Blob in a CBOR library would not be the same as a Blob in another library, despite the same name. And there's a reason why Roc don't have a builtin Blob.
When you say "another library" what kind of library are you referring to? A Roc library?
Yes.

I still don't understand your difficulty. If your other library needs the Blob represented as U64s or whatever, write a function to convert your representation before calling the library. I must be missing something here.

Encapsulation.

The problem is that this bstr problem is just one thing. CBOR is complex, because it can represent every data layout and type that is needed most of the time. This is just one thing out of many. I don't want to restructure my types and program logic just because a serialization library can't keep up.

I would rather write manual serialization, which can be encapsulated, then write the rest of the program normally.
I think you could do an Elm-style encoder/decoder library for CBOR. Then you have full control about how particular types are encoded and decoded.

I already said that:

I would rather write manual serialization, which can be encapsulated, then write the rest of the program normally.

But then why have encoder_for/parser_for if everything has to be manually serialized? And it's not just CBOR, but a bunch of other formats too.

notramo said:

But then why have encoder_for/parser_for if everything has to be manually serialized?

As a convenience for other use cases where a default serialization is good enough.
So basically JSON only?
Why would it be JSON only?
What other serialization format do you know that the builtin can properly handle?

Ziggy? No.
TOML? No.
YAML? No.
CBOR? No.
Gura? No.
JSON is the simplest one, and basically every serialization format has more features than JSON.

Having a default encoding/decoding strategy for any of those formats is valuable even if the encoding doesn't fully exercise every feature of the serialization format. For many use cases that default will be good enough. Anyone is free to define custom encoders/decoders if they feel that for their particular use case the juice is worth the squeeze.

I can understand why @notramo is a bit frustrated here. It should be as simple as adding one more field to the API where you can indicate the type. Is the default encoding/decoding strategy so simple that you don't want to taint it with any extra moving parts?

The only problem with it is that the encoder does not get enough info about the encoded data. I would add a config option to the encoder, for example, to encode e.g. User.public_key as a blob, but it does not know that it's currently encoding User.public_key.

The current API allows encoders/decoders to be configurable. For instance: consider configuring the JSON encoder to tell it whether to produce pretty or compact JSON.

But if you have a custom datatype in which you want to encode some fields one way and another field of the same type a different way, the example @notramo brought at the start of this thread, then I think a custom encoder is your only option. Though maybe the custom encoder can call on the default encoder for parts of the data structure that do not require special handling.
@notramo I had Claude take a stab at this. See what you think about https://github.com/showell/roc-apps/tree/master/cbor-pets (updated after further discussion)
Thanks. I like the simplicity of the parser/encoder, but how does it plug into the default serialization system?

An ideal API would be something like this:

profile : Profile
profile = Cbor.parse(serialized_bytes)

It doesn't plug into the default serialization system, which I think is fine.

I don't understand how you would expect the code below to make sense in Roc. For Cbor.parse to make sense, it has to return a very generic type. The compiler should complain if you're assigning arbitrary data to a concrete type like Profile.

profile : Profile
profile = Cbor.parse(serialized_bytes)

The compiler should complain if you're assigning arbitrary data to a concrete type like Profile.

No, the default parsing mechanism derives the expected shape of the parseable data from the destination type.

This is how JSON parsing works in the stdlib too.
If the CBOR blob do not match the data structure, parse() returns an error that tells that it expected e.g. a string, but found an integer in the encoded CBOR.
I think with the caveat that it would be Cbor.parse(...)?, if that's the mixup Steve?

notramo said:

The compiler should complain if you're assigning arbitrary data to a concrete type like Profile.

No, the default parsing mechanism derives the expected shape of the parseable data from the destination type.

This is how JSON parsing works in the stdlib too.

Do you have an example of that? That's where I wish the docs were a bit more clear.

Sorry, the result should be a Try:

profile : Try(Profile, _)
profile = Cbor.parse(serialized_bytes)
https://github.com/roc-lang/roc/blob/main/docs/langref/parsers.md

Also:
https://www.roc-lang.org/examples/Json/README

Jonathan said:

I think with the caveat that it would be Cbor.parse(...)?, if that's the mixup Steve?

I don't understand your question. I'm asking how Roc type-checks profile = Cbor.parse(serialized_bytes) when you say in the line above that profile has to be the type of Profile.
Roc's type inference is two-way. (Hindley-Millner)
A function can basically ask "What type I'm expected to return?"

The type can be inferred from later uses of a variable.
For example:

# It has to be something that has a .name field, because later it's accessed.
my_var = ...

my_var.name

Steve Howell said:

Jonathan said:

I think with the caveat that it would be Cbor.parse(...)?, if that's the mixup Steve?

I don't understand your question. I'm asking how Roc type-checks profile = Cbor.parse(serialized_bytes) when you say in the line above that profile has to be the type of Profile.

Sorry Steve, that wasn't clear - I just meant that the parse returns a Try(type, err), hence my adding a ? to parse, which is where the parser can complain if your type doesnt match the expected shape.
I recommend pointing an LLM at the Roc repo and ask how the Json.parse uses the two-way type inference to extract the desired type from the return type.
It's a bit complex, but an LLM can explain it quite well.

From Claude:

It also shows exactly where his problem sits: the type is the only instruction the format receives. A List(U8) field always arrives as parse_list_start followed by parse_u8 per element, and there is no parse_bytes hook. So pet_ages and a picture stored as plain List(U8) look identical to the format.

Your example is the exception, because the picture is already an ImageBlob. ImageBlob could define its own parser_for/encoder_for whose where clause asks the format for parse_bytes/encode_bytes; this is Jonathan's suggestion from the thread. JSON would then fail to compile for Profile, which is arguably correct, and CBOR would work. That case is covered; notramo's objection is specifically about two plain List(U8) fields.
Ok, https://github.com/showell/roc-apps/blob/master/cbor-pets/ImageBlob.roc shows Claude's new approach.

Yes, this works, but it requires a custom type, ImageBlob in this case.

But it's very limited in flexibility.

What use case can't it handle? I don't think requiring an ImageBlob class is a workaround here. Do you have some kind of use case where you're hurling blobs around without caring about their actual semantics?
How to serialize a List(U8) field in a type that is from a 3rd party package, so I can't extend it?
Can you give a more concrete example? What if my Profile were in a 3rd party package? Are you claiming you couldn't use it then?
FYI I opened #11727 and #11728 (from Claude) just doing this exercise.
Imagine if Profile were in a 3rd party package, and the image was a List(U8).

I would avoid 3rd party packages that don't distinguish images from ordinary lists of integers. In fact, I don't love that my Profile class models pet ages as List U8 instead of adding a nominal Age type.

I know that sounds like a cop-out, but do you actually have a 3rd party package in mind?

To be a little more pragmatic, if I have a third party package that does a lot of good stuff under the hood, it's almost always the case that I write some kind of edge layer anyway. So that's what I would do here.

adding a nominal Age type.

Yes, that's good practice.

I know that sounds like a cop-out, but do you actually have a 3rd party package in mind?

No specific library. I think, instead of searching for the perfect CBOR library, I'll try a few approaches, and see what's the most usable in practice.
